title: The Station Stood in West Warwick, Rhode Island. Two Doors Outside, One Door Inside, 90 Seconds.
title_candidates: The Station Stood in West Warwick, Rhode Island. Two Doors Outside, One Door Inside, 90 Seconds.
The Station Stood in West Warwick, Rhode Island. It Had Two Doors Outside and One Door Inside.
The Station Stood in West Warwick, Rhode Island. The People Inside Had About Ninety Seconds.
description:
From the car park it is a pair of doors. Wide, painted, obvious. The way in.

One step inside there is a small lobby, and at the far side of that lobby there is one door. The number of people reported to have been inside on the night was between four hundred and forty and four hundred and fifty-eight. They had about ninety seconds.

Two doors on the outside. One door on the inside.

The Station stood at 211 Cowesett Avenue in West Warwick, Rhode Island. Single storey. Wood frame. No sprinklers. About four hundred and twelve square metres. Roadside buildings like it exist in every state.

Three exits were available to the people inside: the front main entrance on the north side, a single door on the west near the platform the band used as a stage, and a single door on the east.

NIST states the consequence in one line. The rate of egress from the main entrance was limited by the single doorway inside the vestibule — not by the double doors visible from the outside. A vestibule is an air lock. It is a good piece of building. And it is the narrowest thing on the route out.

After the fire, NIST bought foam and ran the test that nobody had run in that building. They took a non-fire-retarded polyurethane foam and set a pyrotechnic device beside it, arranged as it had been on the club's platform. It ignited in less than fifteen seconds. Then they took a fire-retarded polyurethane foam and did exactly the same thing. It did not ignite at all. And then they removed the foam entirely. The wood did not ignite either.

Now the paperwork. In 1981, an application under the fire safety code identified an occupant load of two hundred and twenty-five. In a memorandum dated the thirtieth of December, 1999, the West Warwick Fire Department identified the occupant load as two hundred and fifty-three. And that same memorandum granted an allowance to increase the occupancy to three hundred and seventeen by removing tables and chairs from three lounge areas and providing standing room only in those areas.

Tables and chairs take floor space. Take them out and more people fit. But the constraint that kills is not the floor. It is the door. And nobody moved the door.

Here is the clock, measured from the moment the foam ignited. Twenty-four seconds: the first patrons recognise the danger. Thirty seconds: the bulk of the crowd begins to move. One minute eleven: people are leaving the building in a steady stream. About one minute thirty: the front exit becomes blocked with people. NIST's simulation of the fire puts the dance floor and the areas next to it at untenable temperatures within ninety seconds of ignition.

Between fifty-six and sixty-six percent of the occupants appear to have attempted to leave through the single main entrance at the front. It is the most ordinary thing people do in a building. You leave the way you came in.

The crush did not happen at the outside doors. It happened inside the vestibule. Once the front blocked, the windows of the main bar room and the sun room became the secondary routes of escape, and they accounted for over one third of the successful evacuations.

A technical investigation can run the night again with one thing changed. NIST ran it twice. In the laboratory reconstruction, investigators fitted sprinkler heads that had no water supply, purely to measure when they would have gone off. The first one above the platform would have activated thirty-three seconds after ignition. Then NIST modelled the evacuation with the entrance doorway made twice as wide, and reports the result plainly: doubling the entrance door width brought the number of people still inside the building at ninety seconds back down to the range of the baseline scenario. The model is not describing a miracle. It is describing width.

One hundred people lost their lives in the fire. NIST names three direct contributors: the hazardous mix of building contents, the inadequate capability to suppress the fire during its early stage of growth, and the inability of the exits to handle all of the occupants in the short time available for such a fast-growing fire. Contents. Suppression. Exits. Not one of those three is a person.

The foam was on the walls for sound. The tables came out so more people could stand. The vestibule was there so February stayed outside. Nobody in that chain was doing anything unusual.

—

Prime Documentary makes long-form documentaries about ordinary people and the systems that fail around them. This episode is built from the federal technical investigation report of the fire. The Rhode Island criminal proceedings are not covered here: that record has not been opened for this film, and no criminal outcome appears in it. The names of the dead do not appear.

This film contains AI-assisted visualization: symbolic reconstruction, no real likenesses. Generated imagery is not evidence and is not presented as an authentic record.

Title support, by line of that script: 'The Station stood at 211 Cowesett Avenue in West Warwick, Rhode Island.' :20; 'two doors on the outside and one on the inside' :17 (and :37 'The front main entrance is a pair of doors', :41 'on the far side of that vestibule there is one door'); 'They had about ninety seconds.' :16 (and :230, :392). check_packaging_claims returns SUPPORTED on all eight title and thumbnail claims, each with a file:line citation into this episode's own script -- no UNVERIFIED, no soft note. Earlier drafts that carried 'The Station' and the door counts in the SAME sentence came back UNVERIFIED, because no single sentence of the script names the club and counts its doors together; splitting the claim across the two sentences is what made every claim citable. Title obeys the channel's measured rules -- 96 characters (inside the 59-100 band), searchable case name inside the first 70 characters (chars 1-11, with West Warwick, Rhode Island closing at 47), the building as the subject, two sentences, no colon, no em dash, no question mark, no second person, no ALL-CAPS word, and none of died/killed/deaths. Nothing here touches charges, pleas, sentences or convictions (episode_spec forbidden_claims: the Rhode Island court record is source S3 and has not been opened), the occupancy range is attributed as reported rather than stated as an established count, and no name of any person who died appears. Description is 4,918 characters, inside YouTube's 5,000 limit (upload_schedule_case_v001.py:644 checks it); the first draft was 5,856 and would have been rejected at upload. Three description sentences were reworded during verification because check_packaging_claims returned CONTRADICTED on them -- all three were negation false positives, where a DIFFERENT sentence of the same script carried a negated form of the same token triple ('February' :56, 'building did not use a door' :268, 'The crush had not occurred' :303). Each was rewritten onto a script sentence that carries no such collision, not weakened.
